unit.title: SwiftUI bootcamp: delivery and verification
unit.summary: Take a practice feature from shared dependencies and navigation through accessible layout, storage, testing, and an honest handoff.

lessons.title: Environment, dependencies, ViewModifier, and ButtonStyle
lessons.summary: Supply values to a chosen part of the view tree. Reuse card and button appearance while keeping model ownership and button actions clear.
objectives: Define a named environment value and supply it to a view's descendants.
Explain who owns a dependency separately from how children find it.
Reuse decoration with ViewModifier and preserve its modifier order.
Use ButtonStyle for appearance while the Button keeps its action.

sections.title: Supply values to the views that need them
sections.html:
The environment carries values from a view's surrounding hierarchy to its descendants. A subtree is one view and everything beneath it. An override changes values in that subtree. Built-in examples include appearance, text size, locale, and dismissal actions. Compose CompositionLocal offers a familiar scoped-value idea, with different APIs. SwiftUI's environment is not a process-wide dictionary or a factory that creates every model. Ask where the value is supplied and which descendants read it. The owner of a reference still decides how long that instance should remain alive.

This complete example targets an iOS 17+ scratch app using Xcode 15 or later. Replace the generated app and root declarations, keeping one entry. It supplies a synthetic copy configuration through a custom environment key and reuses decoration through a ViewModifier. A ButtonStyle customizes one semantic Button. All types and resources are included; no company dependency container or lab filename is required.

Use an initializer for a dependency that is part of a small component's explicit contract. Use environment when a value is genuinely scoped to a larger subtree and repeated plumbing would obscure that contract. Neither choice decides how long a reference dependency should live. If an app supplies a shared service or observable model, its owner still constructs and retains it deliberately. Environment gives consumers access, not a persistence or cancellation policy.

sections.title: Give the environment value a type and default
sections.html:
An environment key defines a typed slot and its fallback value. EnvironmentKey requires defaultValue. Here LessonCopyKey provides safe made-up copy. The EnvironmentValues extension gives the slot a readable property name with a getter and setter. self[LessonCopyKey.self] accesses that slot using the key type itself. .self means the type value in this expression. This avoids a handwritten String key whose spelling might vary. The default lets an unconfigured consumer read a value, but you must still decide whether missing setup is legitimate for a real dependency.

import SwiftUI

struct LessonCopy {
    var heading: String
    var explanation: String
    static let standard = LessonCopy(
        heading: "Demo reading room",
        explanation: "Synthetic local dependency"
    )
}

private struct LessonCopyKey: EnvironmentKey {
    static let defaultValue = LessonCopy.standard
}

extension EnvironmentValues {
    var lessonCopy: LessonCopy {
        get { self[LessonCopyKey.self] }
        set { self[LessonCopyKey.self] = newValue }
    }
}

struct LearningCardModifier: ViewModifier {
    func body(content: Content) -> some View {
        content
            .padding(16)
            .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)
            .background(.blue.opacity(0.1),
                        in: RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 12))
    }
}

extension View {
    func learningCard() -> some View {
        modifier(LearningCardModifier())
    }
}

struct LearningButtonStyle: ButtonStyle {
    @Environment(\.isEnabled) private var isEnabled

    func makeBody(configuration: Configuration) -> some View {
        configuration.label
            .padding(.horizontal, 16)
            .padding(.vertical, 12)
            .frame(minHeight: 44)
            .background(.blue, in: RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 10))
            .foregroundStyle(.white)
            .opacity(isEnabled ? 1 : 0.45)
            .scaleEffect(configuration.isPressed ? 0.97 : 1)
    }
}

struct DependencyScreen: View {
    @Environment(\.lessonCopy) private var copy
    @Environment(\.colorScheme) private var colorScheme
    @State private var count = 0

    var body: some View {
        VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 16) {
            VStack(alignment: .leading) {
                Text(copy.heading).font(.title2)
                Text(copy.explanation)
                Text(colorScheme == .dark ? "Dark appearance" : "Light appearance")
            }
            .learningCard()
            Button("Practice event: \(count)") { count += 1 }
                .buttonStyle(LearningButtonStyle())
        }
        .padding()
    }
}

@main
struct DependenciesLessonApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            DependencyScreen()
                .environment(\.lessonCopy, .standard)
        }
    }
}

#Preview("Alternate copy") {
    DependencyScreen()
        .environment(\.lessonCopy, LessonCopy(
            heading: "Demo quiet room", explanation: "Preview fixture override"
        ))
}

The \.lessonCopy syntax is a key path naming the EnvironmentValues property. @Environment reads that slot from the current hierarchy. The app installs the standard value outside DependencyScreen. The preview overrides it for its own subtree without changing a global singleton or the screen's source. LessonCopy is a struct, so this configuration is value data rather than a shared mutable reference model.

This key's default is safe made-up copy. A critical service needs a more explicit missing-dependency rule. Quietly constructing a production singleton, a globally shared instance, could start unintended work. A no-op, an implementation that does nothing, might hide missing setup. You could instead make absence optional and display a configuration error, or require a host that supplies the service. Decide whether absence is valid for that feature. EnvironmentKey's required default value does not make that decision for you.

sections.title: Read current values from the view hierarchy
sections.html:
A consumer is a view that reads a supplied value. SwiftUI supplies its environment when the view participates in the hierarchy. Do not assume its initializer can already read the final ancestor override and use it to seed permanent state. A seed is the starting value for new storage; a copied seed can go stale when the environment later changes. Read current display configuration while describing the view. If a model needs a construction input, pass it explicitly to the place that creates and owns the model.

colorScheme is a built-in environment value for light or dark appearance. It uses the same key-path access shape as lessonCopy. The preview can override both at its own boundary. A preview that creates DependencyScreen directly does not automatically inherit everything the app's WindowGroup supplies. If the screen later requires a shared model, also supply that model to its preview. An independent component still needs a complete set of dependencies in each host.

For iOS 17 Observation models, SwiftUI also supports type-based environment distribution with .environment(model) and a typed Environment read. That differs from the custom key-path value mechanism shown here, and legacy EnvironmentObject expects ObservableObject. Do not mix these systems merely because they contain the word environment. When editing a distributed observable model, create the appropriate Bindable access rather than expecting every Environment wrapper to project all nested controls automatically.

sections.title: Reuse the card's decoration
sections.html:
A ViewModifier is a type that wraps a view description with shared behavior or appearance. Its body(content:) receives the content being modified. The framework defines that Content type; it is separate from InfoCard's generic Content in lesson 073. Here the method adds padding, an expanded frame, and background in that order. A View extension offers the convenient learningCard call. You can now reuse that visual rule while still tracing exactly what it changes. It creates no draft owner and starts no loading operation.

The modifier supplies no network service and creates no draft state. That restraint makes it easy to apply to a title group, a summary or a fixture without unexpected lifecycle work. A modifier can contain state or environment reads when those are part of its real responsibility, but a reusable visual card should not become an invisible feature coordinator. Document such responsibilities when they exist.

Changing the modifier changes every caller that uses it, so its layout contract matters. Here it expands to offered width and aligns its child leading. If a caller expects a small content-hugging badge, that modifier may be the wrong abstraction. Reuse is valuable when behavior matches, not merely when two chains contain the same number of dots. Keep adaptive and accessibility requirements visible at the reusable boundary.

sections.title: Style a Button and leave its action with the Button
sections.html:
A ButtonStyle controls how a Button looks. Its Configuration contains the existing label and whether the button is pressed. makeBody uses those values to describe appearance. The Button's original action still changes count, and Button still supplies normal activation behavior. Adding another tap gesture inside the style can duplicate work or disrupt interaction. Keep the product event in the action that owns it. A repeated look is useful to share; it does not justify hiding submit logic inside every control's decoration.

isEnabled tells the style whether the Button is disabled. isPressed supplies temporary press feedback. A minimum height leaves room for the label to grow; it is not a claim that all accessibility requirements passed. The blue and white colors are sample choices that need actual contrast checks in a product. Test disabled, pressed, focus, and large-text cases. The style's job is to reflect those states clearly while keeping the control usable.

SwiftUI's built-in styles are often enough. Create a custom style when the app needs a consistent control contract, and test focus, disabled, pressed and large-text states. PrimitiveButtonStyle exposes deeper activation control and requires additional responsibility; this first example deliberately uses ordinary ButtonStyle. The difference is similar to styling an Android button versus replacing its entire input implementation, although the APIs are not exact counterparts.

sections.title: Trace an override or style that did not apply
sections.html:
An override replaces an inherited environment value for a particular subtree. If the alternate preview still shows standard copy, check where its override is attached and which key the child reads. An override on a sibling does not reach this view. If a model keeps old copy, check whether it stored a seed during initialization. If a disabled Button still looks active, inspect the style's isEnabled read. Follow the value or appearance path that failed before changing the event action or adding another global dependency.

The repository's address view applies project-specific mezzanine text and card modifiers, providing a verified example of scoped visual reuse. Those helpers require company modules and may carry additional policy, so this scratch learningCard is independent. Read the actual wrapper behavior before assuming a same-looking chain has identical sizing or analytics effects. Source presence is not rendering evidence.

Run standard and alternate copy scenarios, then apply disabled to the Button and inspect interaction plus appearance. Verify that only the targeted subtree changes. A useful handoff explains where configuration is supplied, where it is read, what the card changes, and who owns the counter action. That separates dependency access from visual reuse without hiding their practical connections.

acceptance: Overrides apply to the intended descendants.

exercise.solution:
Place two DependencyScreen instances in a VStack. Apply alternate lessonCopy only to the second. The first inherits Demo reading room; the second reads its nearer Demo quiet room value. Each screen's private count remains a separate State value. This scoped display change does not create a shared counter or a persistent model.

Add .disabled(true) to the styled Button for the disabled fixture. Its action should not activate through normal user interaction and the style should use reduced opacity. Remove that fixture afterward or name it explicitly in a preview. The card remains content → padding → expanded frame → background. If you replace LessonCopy with a reference service, choose a host that owns the instance and install it at the intended feature scope; do not construct it inside the visual modifier. The worked record should identify the actual rendered states and leave contrast, focus and assistive checks pending until observed. The native companion's filenames remain its author's responsibility.

lessons.title: Tabs, typed navigation, and split selection
lessons.summary: Keep tab choice, pushed screens, and selected records separate. Use typed routes and recover when a note is missing.
objectives: Name separate owners for the selected tab, push path, and split-view record selection.
Register a route type inside the stack that should open it.
Show a useful state when a selected record no longer exists.
Check narrow and wide navigation and write an explicit restoration rule.

sections.title: Name three different ways to move
sections.html:
Navigation state records where the user is. A tab selects a top-level area. A push path records deeper destinations in a stack. A split selection chooses the record shown in a detail column. SwiftUI offers TabView, NavigationStack, and NavigationSplitView for these different relationships. Android navigation gives a familiar starting distinction. Avoid one Boolean that tries to represent every movement. Each state needs an owner and a rule for how it changes. NavigationSplitView also adapts column presentation, so the same selected ID may be shown differently in a narrow or wide window.

The complete example targets a scratch iOS 17+ app using Xcode 15 or later. NavigationStack and NavigationSplitView arrived in iOS 16; the track keeps its iOS 17 baseline. It uses the broadly supported tabItem form rather than assuming newer Tab APIs are available. Replace the generated app/root declarations with the complete source, keeping one entry. The forced unwraps are restricted to two fixed, valid fixture UUID strings; external route input must be parsed safely.

Browse demonstrates a typed push path, and Settings contains a split-selection practice screen. The label Settings is a teaching top-level area rather than a claim about standard app settings behavior. We want distinct owners for tab, path and selection, not a complete production router. The references and older session 010 provide further navigation study after these basics.

sections.title: Store the destination as a typed value
sections.html:
A route is a value describing where to go. LibraryRoute is an enum; its note case carries a UUID identifying a record. Hashable supplies equality and hashing. Swift can synthesize those because UUID supports them. The path [LibraryRoute] can store this route family. NavigationLink supplies a value to the surrounding stack. navigationDestination says how values of that type become view descriptions. This separates the user's destination choice from the code that builds its content. The route contains a record ID, not a copied mutable record.

import Foundation
import SwiftUI

struct RouteNote: Identifiable {
    let id: UUID
    let title: String
}

enum LibraryRoute: Hashable {
    case note(UUID)
}

enum LibraryTab: Hashable {
    case browse, settings
}

struct RouteDetail: View {
    let id: UUID
    let notes: [RouteNote]
    var body: some View {
        if let note = notes.first(where: { $0.id == id }) {
            Text(note.title).padding().navigationTitle("Detail")
        } else {
            Text("This note is no longer available").padding()
        }
    }
}

struct BrowseStack: View {
    let notes: [RouteNote]
    @State private var path: [LibraryRoute] = []

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack(path: $path) {
            List(notes) { note in
                NavigationLink(note.title, value: LibraryRoute.note(note.id))
            }
            .navigationTitle("Browse")
            .navigationDestination(for: LibraryRoute.self) { route in
                switch route {
                case .note(let id):
                    VStack {
                        RouteDetail(id: id, notes: notes)
                        Button("Return to browse") { path.removeAll() }
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

struct SplitBrowser: View {
    let notes: [RouteNote]
    @State private var selection: UUID?

    var body: some View {
        NavigationSplitView {
            List(notes, selection: $selection) { note in
                NavigationLink(value: note.id) { Text(note.title) }
            }
            .navigationTitle("Library")
        } detail: {
            if let id = selection {
                RouteDetail(id: id, notes: notes)
            } else {
                Text("Select a synthetic note").padding()
            }
        }
    }
}

struct NavigationRoot: View {
    @State private var tab: LibraryTab = .browse
    private let notes = [
        RouteNote(id: UUID(uuidString: "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001")!,
                  title: "Demo ownership"),
        RouteNote(id: UUID(uuidString: "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000002")!,
                  title: "Demo layout")
    ]

    var body: some View {
        TabView(selection: $tab) {
            BrowseStack(notes: notes)
                .tabItem { Label("Browse", systemImage: "books.vertical") }
                .tag(LibraryTab.browse)
            SplitBrowser(notes: notes)
            .tabItem { Label("Settings", systemImage: "gear") }
            .tag(LibraryTab.settings)
        }
    }
}

@main
struct NavigationLessonApp: App {
    var body: some Scene { WindowGroup { NavigationRoot() } }
}

LibraryRoute.self supplies the type for destination registration. .note(let id) reads the case's stored UUID in the switch. RouteDetail then looks for that ID among current notes. If none exists, it displays a recovery message. Clearing path returns Browse to its root, and system Back updates the bound path too. The route says which record was intended; the data lookup decides what can actually be shown now.

Destination registration tells the stack how to turn a route value into content. Place it in the intended stack's hierarchy and outside lazily created rows. Lazy means a row may be created only when needed, so a registration inside it may not exist when a route needs resolving. If a value link does nothing, check its stack and the registered route type first. Adding another nested stack can create a second owner without fixing the missing registration. The route type and its registration scope are part of the behavior.

sections.title: Keep tab choice separate from pushes
sections.html:
A tab is a top-level area, not another pushed destination. TabView binds selection to LibraryTab. Each tab has a tag of that same enum type. The tag is the selected value, while the label is visible text and an image. Translating a label does not need to change tab identity. Tab appearance can vary by iOS and device, so do not base the state model on one screenshot. In this example, choosing Settings changes the tab value; it does not append a Settings record to BrowseStack's path.

BrowseStack owns its own push path. Selecting another tab should not be implemented by appending a Settings route to that path, because it changes a different state domain. For multiple navigation-heavy tabs, give each its intended stack owner and decide whether switching tabs preserves or resets their paths. A global singleton router is unnecessary for this small hierarchy and can make independent navigation lifetimes harder to explain.

Settings uses SplitBrowser directly because the split view already manages its column navigation. Adding another surrounding stack without an independent push flow would create unnecessary ownership and could produce confusing back behavior or duplicate toolbars. Give each top-level area the navigation scope it actually needs. When adding a new destination, explain which container resolves it and which state records it before changing the visual hierarchy.

sections.title: Use a selected ID to show detail
sections.html:
An optional value can hold a value or be nil. SplitBrowser's optional UUID holds the selected note ID. Its List selection binding connects row choice to that detail. Nil shows Select a synthetic note. A nonnil ID whose record is missing shows a different message from RouteDetail. Keep those cases distinct: no choice yet and a choice that cannot be resolved. Stable IDs let order and labels change without redirecting selection to another record. This sample's records are immutable, while a real store also needs to reconcile deletions and account changes.

NavigationSplitView can collapse columns in a compact window, such as a phone, and show multiple columns when space permits. It is not a guarantee that every iPad always presents two columns; window size, platform adaptation and column policy matter. Test selection and return behavior in both compact and expanded configurations. Do not use UIScreen's full-device width as a proxy for the current window's navigation arrangement.

If records are deleted or an account changes, the owner must reconcile selection. It can clear an invalid ID or show a removed-record state with a clear recovery action. Stable record IDs prevent selection jumping when display order changes. A mutable title or row index cannot provide that contract. The beginner example uses immutable synthetic records, while a real store should validate route and selection IDs against current data.

sections.title: Treat restart and outside links as extra work
sections.html:
Restoration means rebuilding navigation after the previous in-memory state is gone. A typed path makes routes easier to inspect, but it does not save them automatically. Encoding, schema versioning, current record checks, and authentication gates are separate rules. NavigationPath can hold different route value types, but one enum is enough for this feature. Use the simpler typed array until the real destination needs call for more flexibility. A saved valid UUID also does not prove the current user may access that note; restoration must check current data and scope.

External links are untrusted inputs. Parse identifiers without force-unwrapping them, check which records are accessible and resolve ownership before constructing a destination. A correct hash or a valid UUID format does not authorize access to a record. Restoring a route whose record was deleted should produce a recoverable state, not a crash. The two literal fixture unwraps in NavigationRoot are not a model for external parsing.

The verified booking demo ContentView uses destination-based links, constructing the destination directly. That simpler form is reasonable for a small static menu. The typed-value form here adds a model for programmatic path changes and intent-based routing. Reading both patterns does not establish that the company app uses one universal router or that every SwiftUI screen owns its own stack.

sections.title: Test each owner and missing-record case
sections.html:
A compact window is one with less room for columns. An expanded window can show more of the split arrangement. Open a Browse note, use Back, then open it again and use Return to browse. Check that its path becomes empty. Switch tabs and record whether the intended Browse state is preserved. In the split area, select the second row and compare detail and Back behavior in available narrow and wide windows. These are separate navigation checks. Changing a tab, popping a stack, and changing selection should each have an explainable owner.

Inject an unknown UUID into a RouteDetail fixture and confirm the unavailable-message branch. Inspect which container owns the Browse stack and which owns the split columns; confirm the split tab has no redundant surrounding stack. If navigation appears twice, look for overlapping container ownership or repeated event triggers. If the wrong note opens after reorder, inspect identity and source resolution.

A useful handoff says that NavigationRoot owns tab selection, BrowseStack owns its route array, and SplitBrowser owns optional row selection. It states which changes preserve each owner and where invalid records recover. These are reviewable behavior contracts. A successful compile does not replace compact/expanded navigation interaction evidence.

steps: Use the complete source in your practice app target.
Open a Browse note, use Back, and test Return to browse.
Select split rows in the narrow and wide window configurations you can actually run.
Explain why the SplitBrowser tab uses its own column navigation without another surrounding stack.

acceptance: Typed route values resolve in the intended stack.
Tab, path and split selection have separately named owners.
The split root uses its own column navigation without a redundant surrounding stack.
Missing records show recovery rather than force-unwrapping external input.
Executed window checks are distinguished from planned ones.
exercise.solution:
Settings uses SplitBrowser directly. That split view manages its columns, while BrowseStack has its own typed push path. For a missing-record fixture, give RouteDetail a valid made-up UUID that matches none of the notes. The lookup should show This note is no longer available. It should not force-unwrap the failed lookup. The fixed UUID literals in the original sample are controlled inputs; use safe parsing for outside links.

A correct route sequence is empty path → one note route → empty path after Back or removeAll. Selecting a tab changes LibraryTab, not that route's record identifier. The split sequence starts with nil, becomes a chosen UUID and resolves its current record. Restoration should validate any stored route against current records and user scope, discarding or recovering invalid destinations. That policy is additional work beyond this in-memory example. Record the actual compact and expanded interactions, including toolbars and return behavior, rather than declaring adaptive navigation passed from one phone screenshot.

simple.story: Ada visits a library with two rooms: Browse and Settings. Choosing a room is one decision. In Browse, she follows a card to a shelf and can walk back along the same path. lessons.title: Sheets, covers, alerts, dialogs, popovers, and dismiss
lessons.summary: Open temporary screens for editing and choices. Keep draft edits separate so Cancel preserves the original, and dismiss from the right view scope.
objectives: Choose and own Boolean or item-based presentation state.
Keep temporary edits in a draft when Cancel must discard them.
Read dismiss inside the presented child so it targets that presentation.
Tell closing apart from saving, destructive choices, and popover adaptation.

sections.title: Choose a temporary screen for a clear job
sections.html:
A presentation is temporary UI shown by an owning view. A sheet can host a richer short flow. A fullScreenCover presents a full-screen flow. An alert gives a small important message. A confirmationDialog offers action choices. A popover supplies contextual content near an anchor. Android dialogs and modal sheets provide a familiar starting idea, but each Apple form has its own interaction and adaptation rules. Choose from the user's job and outcome, rather than only a screenshot. Here the title editor needs a clear distinction between accepting changes and leaving the original intact.

This complete source targets an iOS 17+ scratch app using Xcode 15 or later. Replace the generated app and root declarations, keeping one entry. It contains a staged title editor, a full-screen synthetic guide, an alert, a destructive confirmation and contextual help. Each uses local presentation state, and none accesses a server, persistent store or real account.

Write the outcome contract before the UI: Save commits a trimmed nonempty title, Cancel preserves the original, Clear removes only the in-memory title after confirmation, and the guide's Done simply closes it. An editor closing does not by itself mean Save succeeded. This separation is especially important when interactive dismiss gestures can close a presentation without invoking your explicit buttons.

sections.title: Use a flag or an item to describe what is open
sections.html:
Presentation state records whether temporary UI should be shown and, when needed, what it should edit. A Boolean is enough for the fixed guide. An optional identifiable item combines selection and presentation. EditRequest carries the starting title and a UUID made for this editing interaction. Nil means no edit request. Assigning a request supplies both the reason to open the sheet and its initial content. This avoids a show-editor flag disagreeing with a separate selected title. The owner still needs an explicit rule for what replaces an active draft.

import Foundation
import SwiftUI

struct EditRequest: Identifiable {
    let id = UUID()
    let title: String
}

struct StagedEditor: View {
    @Environment(\.dismiss) private var dismiss
    @State private var draft: String
    let initial: String
    let onSave: (String) -> Void

    init(initial: String, onSave: @escaping (String) -> Void) {
        self.initial = initial
        self.onSave = onSave
        _draft = State(initialValue: initial)
    }

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack {
            Form { TextField("Demo title", text: $draft) }
                .navigationTitle("Edit draft")
                .toolbar {
                    ToolbarItem(placement: .cancellationAction) {
                        Button("Cancel") { dismiss() }
                    }
                    ToolbarItem(placement: .confirmationAction) {
                        Button("Save") {
                            let value = draft.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines)
                            guard !value.isEmpty else { return }
                            onSave(value)
                            dismiss()
                        }
                        .disabled(draft.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines).isEmpty)
                    }
                }
        }
        .interactiveDismissDisabled(draft != initial)
    }
}

struct FullScreenGuide: View {
    @Environment(\.dismiss) private var dismiss
    var body: some View {
        VStack(spacing: 20) {
            Text("Synthetic practice guide").font(.title)
            Button("Done") { dismiss() }
        }
        .padding()
    }
}

struct PresentationScreen: View {
    @State private var title = "Demo reading plan"
    @State private var edit: EditRequest?
    @State private var showGuide = false
    @State private var showAlert = false
    @State private var showDelete = false
    @State private var showHelp = false
    @State private var closeMessage = ""

    var body: some View {
        VStack(spacing: 16) {
            Text(title.isEmpty ? "No plan" : title).font(.title2)
            Button("Edit in sheet") { edit = EditRequest(title: title) }
            Button("Open full-screen guide") { showGuide = true }
            Button("Show synthetic error") { showAlert = true }
            Button("Clear plan", role: .destructive) { showDelete = true }
            Button("Help") { showHelp = true }
                .popover(isPresented: $showHelp) {
                    Text("This is a synthetic draft, stored only in memory.")
                        .padding()
                }
            Text(closeMessage).foregroundStyle(.secondary)
        }
        .padding()
        .sheet(item: $edit, onDismiss: { closeMessage = "Editor closed" }) { request in
            StagedEditor(initial: request.title) { title = $0 }
        }
        .fullScreenCover(isPresented: $showGuide) { FullScreenGuide() }
        .alert("Synthetic error", isPresented: $showAlert) {
            Button("OK", role: .cancel) {}
        } message: {
            Text("No external request was made.")
        }
        .confirmationDialog("Clear the plan?", isPresented: $showDelete,
                            titleVisibility: .visible) {
            Button("Clear", role: .destructive) { title = "" }
            Button("Cancel", role: .cancel) {}
        } message: {
            Text("Only the synthetic in-memory title will be removed.")
        }
    }
}

@main
struct PresentationLessonApp: App {
    var body: some Scene { WindowGroup { PresentationScreen() } }
}

The sheet closure receives the current request. Its callback assigns the saved value to the root's title. FullScreenGuide is a complete child with its own dismissal read. Button roles indicate cancellation or destructive intent, while the product action still decides what data changes. Empty action closures in the alert's OK and dialog's Cancel mean there is no domain mutation beyond the framework presentation's closure behavior.

Give item identities a declared policy. A fresh EditRequest starts a new editing interaction. For a record editor, you might instead use the record's stable ID and handle explicit draft replacement. Do not use a mutable title as identity or rely on replacing the optional item to silently reset unsaved fields. As lesson 075 established, initial state seeds and later input synchronization differ.

sections.title: Keep typing separate until Save
sections.html:
A staged draft is a temporary copy that has not yet changed the parent. StagedEditor keeps that copy in local State. _draft names the underlying State wrapper, and State(initialValue:) supplies its starting value. The initializer also keeps onSave for a later button action. @escaping permits that closure to be used after the initializer returns. (String) -> Void means it receives one String and returns no value. These details show both where edits live and how an accepted value will leave the editor.

Typing changes only draft. Save trims its input, rejects an empty result, calls onSave, then asks the sheet to close. Cancel asks it to close without calling onSave. The parent's title therefore stays intact on Cancel. If you instead pass a live binding to the parent's title, every keystroke already changes it. Naming a button Cancel cannot undo that. Choose staged editing when discard is part of the promised outcome, and keep the commit point visible.

interactiveDismissDisabled blocks the ordinary interactive dismissal gesture when the draft differs from its initial value. It does not prevent our explicit Cancel action from dismissing, and it is not an automatic unsaved-changes confirmation dialog. The teaching policy is that dirty drafts require an explicit Save or Cancel. If a product wants swipe-to-close with a discard prompt, implement that outcome policy deliberately rather than assuming the modifier supplies it.

sections.title: Ask the presented child to close its own scope
sections.html:
A dismissal action uses the presentation context around the view that reads it. @Environment(\.dismiss) obtains that action. StagedEditor and FullScreenGuide read it inside their presented content. The root's earlier dismiss read may belong to another context or do nothing for this sheet. The same API can also pop an appropriate navigation destination. Check where it is read rather than assuming every dismiss call closes the same UI. This example gives each temporary child the action for its own scope.

Calling dismiss requests a UI transition. It is not proof that an animation finished, a server write succeeded or a domain result was delivered exactly once. If a flow starts asynchronous saves, keep the draft active or show saving state until the operation's policy permits closing. Handle save failure without falsely reporting success. This lesson's callback is synchronous and updates only synthetic local state.

onDismiss updates closeMessage when the sheet closes by any supported route. It does not change the parent's title or commit a draft. Closure alone does not tell you whether the user saved, cancelled, or met a failure. A larger flow may use an idempotent finish operation, one that reports a terminal outcome only once even if called again. That outcome can distinguish saved, cancelled, and failed. Lesson 010 traces a coordinator with richer result handling. The first editor here keeps its save callback separate from its close notification.

sections.title: Use messages, choices, and anchored help
sections.html:
An action role tells the platform the intended kind of action, such as cancel or destructive. The alert uses a title, message, and acknowledgment. The confirmation dialog offers Clear and Cancel. Only Clear's action removes the synthetic title. Its role can affect presentation and styling; it does not delete data by itself, authorize another deletion, or create undo storage. Both use Boolean state for visibility. The popover instead attaches help to its anchor, the Help button. Space and platform rules can adapt how that anchored content appears.

The popover attaches to the Help button, giving it an anchor in the hierarchy. In compact presentations, the system may adapt a popover into a sheet or other appropriate form. Test the actual window configuration instead of asserting a floating bubble always appears on a phone. For a design that needs an explicit adaptation preference, study presentationCompactAdaptation, available from iOS 16.4, and its applicable presentation behavior. A preference still needs actual interaction and content checks.

Keep presentation roots stable. Conditional removal of the view that owns a sheet can change its lifetime, and presenting competing flows from unrelated Booleans can create coordination problems. A larger feature may benefit from one presentation enum or optional identifiable route rather than many independent flags. Our flags represent separate user-triggered examples, so avoid triggering several at once and describe any future mutual-exclusion policy.

sections.title: Test each way the presentation can end
sections.html:
A terminal outcome is how a flow finishes: accepted, cancelled, or otherwise closed. Open the editor, type a new title, and Cancel. The parent should keep its original. Reopen and type spaces; Save is disabled and its action also guards invalid input. Enter Demo Lin and Save, then check the parent. Open unchanged content and try a swipe dismissal. Next edit it and check the dirty-dismiss restriction. Dirty means the draft differs from its starting value. Test the guide separately; its Done action closes without editing the title.

Trigger Clear, choose Cancel and verify preservation, then confirm Clear and verify the No plan display. Inspect Help on a compact and wider window if available. These are expected acceptance observations, not recorded execution results in this authored lesson. A compile does not prove the gesture or adaptation paths. Record actual evidence for each terminal outcome.

The active picker demo provides a verified source anchor for presentation ownership through a UIKit host and coordinator. Its architecture is more elaborate than these local SwiftUI presentations, and reading it does not justify copying internal feature views into the scratch target. Use it to compare who reports an outcome and who owns closing. A correct beginner handoff names both, including the difference between Cancel and onDismiss.

exercise.brief: Check Save, Cancel, changed-draft dismissal, and Clear confirmation in the temporary editor.
steps: Use the complete source in a practice app.

exercise.solution:
Typing changes the local draft, so the parent's title still holds the committed value. Save trims and validates before calling onSave. The parent callback assigns the accepted title, and the sheet reads its own dismiss action to request closure. Cancel skips the callback. The chosen rule blocks a changed draft's ordinary swipe dismissal, while explicit Cancel can still discard it. Closing an unchanged editor updates Editor closed without saving anything.

For a swipe-with-confirmation product, introduce an explicit pending-discard outcome and prompt rather than writing to root during typing. For asynchronous saves, add a saving/error state and define when closing is allowed; a dismiss call cannot stand in for successful persistence. The guide is independently closable because it reads its own action. The confirmation Clear path runs only after that selected destructive action; Cancel makes no title assignment. Record actual gesture and popover checks separately from model predictions. Nothing in the source claims a stored record was deleted or an iOS app was executed here.

simple.meaning: A staged sheet owns a temporary draft. Typing changes that draft, and Save explicitly sends a validated value to the parent. Cancel only asks the sheet to close. onDismiss reports closure, not whether a save happened.

Editable input kept apart from committed data until an explicit save.
A function supplied for another component to call when an event happens.

lessons.title: Tasks, onChange, lifecycle, cancellation, and freshness
lessons.summary: Give async work a clear view lifetime. Request cancellation when it becomes old, and check permission before either a result or error changes the screen.
objectives: Use task for view-associated work and choose an onChange signature supported by the target.
Explain why asking work to stop differs from allowing it to update the screen.
Give each request a new token and check it before publishing success or failure.
Plan tests that control completion order and record lifecycle checks separately.

sections.title: Let a task own the waiting work
sections.html:
A task is asynchronous work that can suspend while waiting. SwiftUI's task modifier associates it with a view. The id form can replace that work when its Equatable key changes; Equatable means values can be compared for equality. Compose LaunchedEffect offers a familiar keyed-lifetime idea, but SwiftUI controls the details here. Body describes the interface and may run repeatedly. A request started there has no reliable single-start rule. Choose one task scope for the search, then decide what starts it, asks it to stop, and allows it to publish.

This complete source targets a scratch iOS 17+ app with Xcode 15 or later. It uses Observation and the iOS 17 two-parameter onChange overload. Task itself predates that minimum, but this particular example needs its newer dependencies. Replace the generated App and root declarations, keeping one entry. The service is a synthetic asynchronous fixture with no transport, account or disk operation.

Separate three questions: what starts work, what requests its cancellation, and what permits a result to become current UI? A view-associated task answers part of the lifetime question. Cancellation is cooperative; it does not forcibly terminate every callback or kill a thread. Freshness checks answer the publication question even when obsolete work completes. A correct design needs all three boundaries.

sections.title: Await the operation in the view's task
sections.html:
A work key identifies when this associated task should change. WorkKey includes the request token and whether the scene is active. It is Equatable, so SwiftUI can compare those values. The task captures the current query and token, then awaits model.load directly. It does not start another unstructured Task and return before loading ends. Await permits suspension. Try handles a thrown error. Task.sleep is an asynchronous delay that can cooperate with cancellation; it does not hold a thread asleep while waiting.

import Foundation
import Observation
import SwiftUI

struct WorkKey: Equatable {
    let token: UUID
    let active: Bool
}

enum FixtureFailure: Error { case unavailable }

struct FixtureSearch {
    func search(_ query: String) async throws -> [String] {
        try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(250))
        if query == "fail" { throw FixtureFailure.unavailable }
        return query.isEmpty ? [] : ["Demo result for \(query)"]
    }
}

@MainActor
@Observable
final class SearchState {
    var query = "" {
        didSet {
            guard query != oldValue else { return }
            invalidate()
        }
    }
    private(set) var token = UUID()
    private(set) var results: [String] = []
    private(set) var status = "Enter a synthetic query"

    func invalidate() {
        token = UUID()
        results = []
        status = "Waiting for current request"
    }

    func load(query: String, token expected: UUID,
              service: FixtureSearch) async {
        guard token == expected, !Task.isCancelled else { return }
        status = query.isEmpty ? "No query" : "Loading"
        do {
            let values = try await service.search(query)
            guard token == expected, !Task.isCancelled else { return }
            results = values
            status = values.isEmpty ? "No matches" : "Ready"
        } catch is CancellationError {
            return
        } catch {
            guard token == expected, !Task.isCancelled else { return }
            results = []
            status = "Synthetic request failed"
        }
    }
}

@MainActor
struct TaskScreen: View {
    @Environment(\.scenePhase) private var scenePhase
    @State private var model = SearchState()
    @State private var observedChanges = 0
    private let service = FixtureSearch()

    var body: some View {
        @Bindable var editable = model
        VStack(spacing: 16) {
            TextField("Synthetic query; fail tests the error", text: $editable.query)
                .textFieldStyle(.roundedBorder)
            Text(model.status)
            Text("Observed query changes: \(observedChanges)")
            ForEach(model.results, id: \.self) { Text($0) }
        }
        .padding()
        .task(id: WorkKey(token: model.token, active: scenePhase == .active)) {
            guard scenePhase == .active else { return }
            let expected = model.token
            let query = model.query
            await model.load(query: query, token: expected, service: service)
        }
        .onChange(of: model.query) { _, _ in
            observedChanges += 1
        }
        .onChange(of: scenePhase) { _, phase in
            if phase != .active { model.invalidate() }
        }
        .onDisappear { model.invalidate() }
    }
}

@main
@MainActor
struct TasksLessonApp: App {
    var body: some Scene { WindowGroup { TaskScreen() } }
}

Bindable supplies the TextField projection for the existing SearchState model. It does not create another search source. The query's didSet property observer runs after assignment. It ignores an unchanged value and otherwise calls invalidate before an old completion can publish with the old token. Invalidate gives the next request a new UUID token and clears visible results. This UUID names a generation of work. It is not a saved record key or the identity of a list row.

The service returns a String array or throws FixtureFailure for the explicit fail input. The results' String identities are acceptable only because this fixture returns at most one unique result. A real result list should use stable domain IDs; repeated titles would not be valid unique row keys. The delay makes the demo visibly asynchronous, but it is not a test gate.

sections.title: Check old results as well as cancellation
sections.html:
Cancellation asks work to cooperate in stopping. When a task id changes, SwiftUI cancels the earlier associated task and starts replacement work as appropriate. Leaving the view can also cancel its task under the framework's lifetime. Our sleep-based fixture cooperates. A callback adapter or remote service may still complete or continue elsewhere. Observing a cancelled Swift task is therefore different from proving the producer stopped. Keep a separate publication rule so late results cannot regain permission just because a stop request arrived too late.

Publication means assigning a completion into current screen state. Before publishing either success or failure, the model checks its current token against the captured token and checks Task.isCancelled. An old result cannot replace newer data, and an old error cannot hide it. The CancellationError branch quietly returns. A real transport may report cancellation with another error type, so follow its documented contract too. The token and cancellation checks protect current UI without claiming every producer immediately stops.

A query can change A → B → A while the first A still waits. Call those requests A1, B, and A2. Comparing only text A would wrongly allow A1 to publish again. Each generation therefore needs its own token. Leaving the view or making the scene inactive also invalidates permission, even if old work finishes. MainActor serializes access to this UI state. Await can still suspend one operation while another changes the token. That is actor reentrancy: later work can run during the wait, so recheck permission after it.

sections.title: Give scene and view changes a written rule
sections.html:
onChange runs a handler when a compared value changes. On iOS 17, the two-parameter form provides old and new values; a zero-parameter form is also available. The older onChange(of:perform:) form receives one new value and supports older systems. Match the signature to the target's availability. Here the query handler only increments a diagnostic counter. It does not start another search. That leaves task as the one search trigger and makes duplicate-start bugs easier to find.

A scene is a system-managed presentation scope. scenePhase reports whether that scene is active, inactive, or in background. It is not an Android Activity and does not grant unlimited background time. This sample invalidates publication when inactive. Active state is also in the work key so current work can reload when active again. The task guard prevents inactive loading. A product might preserve results instead of clearing them; state that policy deliberately rather than assuming every scene change must reset a search.

onAppear and onDisappear can occur more than once. Treat them as view-lifetime signals rather than globally unique startup or teardown events. Here disappearance invalidates current publication, complementing task cancellation. It does not destroy the app-owned service or save the draft. For a feature-owned task that must survive navigation, choose another explicit owner and retained handle; attaching it to a transient view would express the wrong lifetime.

sections.title: Control which request finishes first
sections.html:
A deterministic test chooses the order of important events. Start A1 and wait for a fixture signal that it began. Then start B and A2. Release A2 first and check its result. Release A1 afterward and check that the result stays from A2. Repeat with an old failure. A gate is a test-controlled point that holds and releases completion. The fixture must be able to finish despite cancellation, or it might never reach the old-publication guard. A short delay makes a demo visible, but it does not control this test schedule.

Also test an old completion after explicit invalidation without a replacement request. The model should leave it unpublished. Test duplicate starts and ensure one user event does not spawn work from body, onChange and task simultaneously. Track start, completion and publication as separate events. A delay-based screen demo is useful for learning, but it cannot prove deterministic ordering or transport cancellation.

The verified address form uses the iOS 17-style onChange signature for focus and field updates. The member-ID demo starts mock work on appearance, providing a legacy source comparison rather than a pattern to copy indiscriminately. No client code was changed and no production request cancellation was measured in this audit.

sections.title: Find where old output was allowed to publish
sections.html:
The publication boundary is the assignment that changes current UI. If old data appears, inspect the success guard and when token invalidation occurs. Check whether a service bypasses those guards by writing state directly. If an old error hides new data, inspect the catch branch in the same way. If loading starts twice, trace every trigger and key change before adding a throttle. If work continues after leaving, check whether its producer needs a cancellation adapter. A request to cancel and a rejected old publication answer different questions.

If an actor diagnostic appears, carry a safe result back to the MainActor model instead of removing isolation. Actor reentrancy means another request can invalidate the token while the first is suspended. Capture the expected token before await and recheck afterward. A weak capture solves some retention cycles but does not prove freshness or cancel a producer.

Record actual compiler and fixture checks separately from simulator lifecycle interaction. The lesson's source specifies expected behavior; it does not claim the app backgrounded, a callback stopped or every error race was tested. The capstone supplies a concrete completion-gated testing pattern, while larger concurrency adapters remain specialist practice in the existing deep dives.

quiz.question: What does task(id:) cancellation guarantee?
options: Immediate termination of every server operation
A cooperative cancellation request for the associated Swift task
Persistent saving of its current result
quiz.explanation: Producer cancellation and transport behavior need their own contracts.

quiz.question: Why does A → B → A need a request token?
options: Old and new A requests share text but differ in freshness
quiz.explanation: The token distinguishes A1 from A2 and guards obsolete success and error publication.

quiz.question: Which paths need a freshness guard?
options: Both success and failure, plus explicit invalidation policy
quiz.explanation: An obsolete error can be just as harmful as obsolete data.

exercise.brief: Try the view-owned task example. Plan controlled tests for an old success, an old error, and a completion after invalidation.
steps: Use the complete made-up search service and trace each query and token change.
Try an ordinary query and fail. Check available view-leaving or scene-change behavior.
Write the A1, B, A2 start and completion order and the expected visible result.
Plan a fixture with start signals and test-controlled success or error completion, even after cancellation.
List work triggers and keep the search operation in task rather than also starting it in body or onChange.
acceptance: No request begins from body or the query onChange diagnostic.
Success and failure commits both require the current token and uncancelled task.
Invalidation revokes publication even without a replacement query.

exercise.solution:
Give A1, B, and A2 distinct tokens. Let A2 publish first. A later A1 success or error must leave A2's output unchanged. Query didSet invalidates synchronously, so matching the current text A is not enough for A1. The key also includes active state: becoming active can restart current work, while inactive guards block loading. Explicit invalidation changes the token even when no replacement result will be requested. Check that this also rejects a later completion.

A worked test design retains one completion continuation per request and records a start signal. Start A1, await its signal, start A2 under a new token, await that signal, finish A2 successfully and await its load completion, then finish A1 and await it. Assert current output again. Repeat with old failure and with invalidation-only. The fixture intentionally ignores cancellation to exercise the token guard; every continuation must still be resumed during cleanup. Do not infer that a remote producer stopped from these UI assertions. Record the actual test execution separately. The source delay is a visual fixture, not that deterministic test.

simple.story: Ada asks a bakery for loaf A and receives ticket 1. She changes her order to B and receives ticket 2. Then she asks for A again and receives ticket 3. Ada tells the baker to stop the earlier orders, but they may already be in the oven. When loaf A for ticket 1 arrives, its name matches her latest choice. Its ticket does not. Ada accepts only ticket 3. The same rule applies if an older order arrives with an error note rather than a loaf.
simple.meaning: Cancellation requests cooperation from old work. A request token separately decides whether a completion may update current UI. The A1 → B → A2 sequence needs distinct tokens because text A alone cannot distinguish the two A requests.

example.before: A controlled fixture started A1, B, and A2 with tokens t1, t2, and t3. A2 has already published Current A2. A1 is still waiting, and t3 is current.
example.change: Release A1 successfully with the value Old A1.
example.after: Current A2 remains displayed. A1's captured token t1 does not match t3, even though both requests used query A. A separate old-error release must also leave the current result intact.

picture.caption: An older A completion cannot replace the newest A after the query changes away and back.

items.label: Start A1
items.text: Query A starts with token t1.

items.label: Start B then A2
items.text: Each input change creates a new token; t3 is now current.

items.label: Finish A2
items.text: A matching token and uncancelled task permit its result to publish.

items.label: Finish A1
items.text: Token t1 is old, so its result or error cannot replace A2.

words.meaning: An asynchronous unit of work that can suspend while waiting.
A suspension point where the caller waits for an asynchronous operation.
A request for work to cooperate in stopping, rather than an instant forced stop.
A value naming one generation of work and its permission to publish.
Whether a completion still belongs to the current request.
Rules that serialize access to actor-protected state, with no promise of a dedicated thread.

simple.remember: Ask old work to stop, and independently reject its old results and errors.
simple.boundary: Tickets are only a model for publication permission. Cancellation does not rewind a remote side effect or kill a thread. MainActor isolation governs safe UI access, but a suspended operation can resume after another request has changed the token.

lessons.title: Adaptive layout, Dynamic Type, localization, and accessibility
lessons.summary: Keep content and actions usable when the window, text size, language direction, or input method changes. Record what you actually checked.
objectives: Use available space and larger text settings without losing content or actions.
Keep controls' accessible roles and group only information that belongs together.
Tell translated resources, locale formatting, and right-to-left layout apart.
Record specific layout and accessibility results and the checks still pending.

sections.title: Use the current window and content
sections.html:
Available space is the room the current view can use. A device name does not tell you that size. An iPad can have a narrow window; a phone can use much larger text. Multitasking, safe areas, keyboard display, and resizing all change usable space. Safe areas are the layout regions that account for surrounding system features. You already make similar Android decisions. In SwiftUI, let content negotiate the offered space. Reading the physical screen's full width and imposing a fixed form width can miss the actual window that contains your view.

This complete example belongs to a scratch iOS 17+ app using Xcode 15 or later. ViewThatFits arrived in iOS 16, and the track keeps its established minimum. Replace the generated App and root types, keeping one entry. It uses system controls, synthetic data and a scrollable container. The source provides a starting layout and test scenarios; it is not certification of accessibility or proof of device execution.

Prefer a layout that negotiates offered space. This example caps a readable content column at six hundred forty points and centers it when more width is available. That value is a teaching design choice, not a platform rule. In a narrow window the parent still constrains available width. Content remains scrollable vertically so large text does not require hiding information to fit a fixed-height card.

sections.title: Offer a readable second arrangement
sections.html:
ViewThatFits selects the first candidate that fits along the chosen dimension. Here it tries a horizontal row, then a vertical column. An ideal size is the content's preferred extent before it is squeezed to fit. The horizontal candidate uses fixedSize to ask for that extent. If it does not fit, the vertical candidate changes the relationship between summary and button. Without that intention, a row might compress words until it technically fits but is hard to read. A fallback should make the same feature usable, not silently remove part of it.

import Foundation
import SwiftUI

struct AdaptiveSummary: View {
    let title: String
    var body: some View {
        VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 8) {
            Text(verbatim: title).font(.title2)
            Text("Synthetic progress").foregroundStyle(.secondary)
        }
        .accessibilityElement(children: .combine)
    }
}

struct AdaptiveScreen: View {
    @Environment(\.dynamicTypeSize) private var textSize
    @State private var reminders = false
    @State private var count = 0
    let title: String

    private var practiceButton: some View {
        Button {
            count += 1
        } label: {
            Label("Practice", systemImage: "book")
                .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, minHeight: 44)
        }
        .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
        .accessibilityHint("Increases the synthetic practice count")
        .accessibilityIdentifier("practiceButton")
    }

    var body: some View {
        ScrollView {
            VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 20) {
                Image(systemName: "books.vertical")
                    .font(.largeTitle)
                    .accessibilityHidden(true)

                if textSize.isAccessibilitySize {
                    VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 16) {
                        AdaptiveSummary(title: title)
                        practiceButton
                    }
                } else {
                    ViewThatFits(in: .horizontal) {
                        HStack(alignment: .top, spacing: 20) {
                            AdaptiveSummary(title: title)
                            practiceButton
                        }
                        .fixedSize(horizontal: true, vertical: false)
                        VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 16) {
                            AdaptiveSummary(title: title)
                            practiceButton
                        }
                    }
                }

                Toggle("Demo reminders", isOn: $reminders)
                Text("Practice count: \(count)")
                    .accessibilityIdentifier("practiceCount")
                Text("No notification is scheduled by this toggle.")
                    .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
            }
            .padding()
            .frame(maxWidth: 640, alignment: .leading)
            .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .center)
        }
    }
}

@main
struct AdaptiveLessonApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup { AdaptiveScreen(title: "Demo learning plan") }
    }
}

#Preview("Long, large, RTL") {
    AdaptiveScreen(title: "A deliberately long synthetic learning plan title")
        .environment(\.dynamicTypeSize, .accessibility3)
        .environment(\.layoutDirection, .rightToLeft)
        .environment(\.locale, Locale(identifier: "ar"))
}

The explicit branch for accessibility text sizes chooses a column even in a wide window. DynamicTypeSize reports the user's text category; isAccessibilitySize identifies its larger categories. It does not detect whether VoiceOver is on. A size class gives a broad compact-or-regular category, rather than an exact local width. Use content fitting or local geometry when precise width matters. Keep title, button, Toggle, and count available in either arrangement.

A fallback must preserve the same feature. Hiding the practice action in the narrow candidate would make the layout appear to fit while removing functionality. A changed arrangement should still expose the title, action, Toggle and count. Avoid shrinking system fonts to force an overflowing title into a screenshot. If text can be long, allow wrapping, vertical growth and scrolling where the product permits.

sections.title: Let larger text have more room
sections.html:
Dynamic Type is the system that follows the user's chosen text-size category. System roles such as title2 and body scale with it. A custom font needs a suitable relative text style or another deliberate scaling rule. A fixed point size alone does not establish that behavior. Also inspect surrounding layout. Fixed heights, narrow frames, line limits, and control labels can clip even when the font itself scales correctly. Give content room to wrap and grow, and use a different arrangement when scaling alone cannot keep it readable.

The practice action uses a minimum height rather than a fixed height, allowing its Label to expand. Forty-four points is a familiar iOS touch-target starting convention, not evidence that every resulting target is accessible. Verify the actual tappable area, spacing between neighboring controls and behavior under larger text. A frame enlarging drawing does not automatically prove hit testing for arbitrary custom gestures; semantic Button behavior is the safer starting point.

ScaledMetric is a SwiftUI wrapper that scales a custom numeric dimension with the text-size environment. Use it when that dimension should grow with text, such as a related icon size. Do not enlarge every gap blindly. A narrow layout may need a column rather than a larger spacer. Try long text at several widths and size categories. Truncation means text has been cut short; record it and any unreachable control as a problem even if the ordinary fixture looks good. Font scaling is only part of a usable layout.

sections.title: Group information and keep actions separate
sections.html:
Accessibility semantics describe an element's role, meaning, state, and actions. AdaptiveSummary combines its title and progress caption into one reading group because they describe one informational unit. The Button and Toggle stay separate so users can operate them. Combining the whole screen into one element would make those interactions harder to find or use. Choose grouping from the information relationship. Reducing the number of VoiceOver stops is useful only when it preserves meaning and reachability. A visual card does not always need to be one accessible element.

The decorative books image is hidden from accessibility because the title already carries its meaning. The practice Button has a visible Label, with a hint explaining its synthetic effect. A hint should add useful behavior information rather than repeat the label. Toggle supplies state semantics automatically. The reminder wording explicitly says no notification is scheduled, avoiding a misleading permission implication.

accessibilityIdentifier is a machine-facing identifier for UI automation. It is not the spoken accessibility label and should not replace readable visible text. The count identifier lets tests locate the value without matching every translated string. Test VoiceOver reading order, labels, states and actions on an appropriate simulator or device, then test keyboard or alternative input where relevant. A screenshot cannot show whether those interactions work.

sections.title: Check translation and direction separately
sections.html:
Localization supplies resources for supported languages. SwiftUI's text literals can participate in localized-key lookup. A user's display name is data rather than a translation key, so Text(verbatim:) states that intent here. The interpolated count supports a structured sentence instead of piecing text together blindly. For real translations, add the needed String Catalog entries to your practice project and check those resources. A locale setting controls formatting and related language behavior. It does not create missing translations by itself.

The preview sets right-to-left layout direction and an Arabic locale. That tests direction and formatting choices, not a translated Arabic interface when only English resources exist. Check leading and trailing alignment and where symbols sit relative to words. Then test translated text through actual catalog resources separately. Label the evidence accurately: RTL fixture rendering, locale formatting, and linguistic correctness are different checks.

Also check increased contrast, light/dark appearance and color distinctions. Do not communicate status only by red versus green or an unlabelled icon. VoiceOver must have meaningful information, and sighted users may need a textual status or shape distinction. Reduce Motion matters for custom animation, although this example has no custom transition. A complete real feature needs a scoped matrix rather than a claim to cover every platform setting.

sections.title: Record a small set of repeatable checks
sections.html:
A verification matrix is a list of chosen conditions and their actual results. Start with ordinary and long titles in narrow and wide windows, then larger text. Add light, dark, and RTL fixtures. For interaction, check that scrolling reaches every control, Practice updates count, Toggle exposes its state, and VoiceOver reads information and actions in the intended order. A screenshot answers visual questions for one case. It cannot show that an action is reachable through a screen reader. Add keyboard and focus checks when the feature includes text fields.

The active address form supplies a verified anchor for explicit field focus and next-field configuration. It is a useful production comparison, but its source does not prove the scratch layout's accessibility behavior. No client files should be edited for this exercise. The workbench's actual files and execution checks remain its author's scope.

For each check, record configuration, actual observation and unresolved issue. Compiler success proves declarations and type relationships under that compiler/SDK, not VoiceOver correctness. Preview rendering proves one visual fixture. Simulator or device interaction supplies another layer. A clear handoff can say visual fixtures inspected, assistive checks pending, and exactly what still needs to run; honest limits make the work useful to another engineer.

ScrollView permits vertical growth, and a minimum control height permits expansion. The summary is one reading group, while actions remain separate controls. Compare these expected relationships with actual rendering and interaction, rather than marking accessibility passed from source alone.
